meta.book_title: metricsAI: An Introduction to Econometrics with Python and AI in the Cloud

practice.concept: Standard error and precision (Section 4.1, Key Concept 4.1)
practice.stem: Suppose a sample of 64 workers has a mean wage of $45,000 and a standard deviation of $16,000. What is the standard error of the mean?

options.feedback: This divides the standard deviation by n = 64. The standard error divides by the square root of n.
$16,000 is the standard deviation, which describes individual wages. The standard error describes the sample mean.
This divides the mean by √64. The standard error is built from the standard deviation, not the mean.

practice.concept: Standard error and precision (Section 4.1, Key Concept 4.1)
practice.stem: Continuing the example (n = 64, standard deviation $16,000, standard error $2,000), what sample size would cut the standard error in half, to about $1,000?

options.feedback: Doubling n divides the standard error by √2 ≈ 1.41, not by 2.
A smaller sample makes the standard error larger, not smaller.
Squaring the sample size divides the standard error by 8 here, far more than needed.
Correct. Halving s/√n requires doubling √n, so n must be multiplied by 4: 4 × 64 = 256.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 4.1: the standard error shrinks at rate 1/√n, so quadrupling the sample size halves it: 16,000/√256 = 16,000/16 = $1,000.

practice.concept: Standard error and precision (Section 4.1, Key Concept 4.1)
practice.stem: Suppose two surveys from the same city estimate mean commute time. Survey A uses 100 commuters and reports a standard error of 1.2 minutes; Survey B uses 400 commuters and reports a standard error of 0.6 minutes. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Survey B's commuters have less variable commute times than Survey A's commuters.
options.feedback: Recover each standard deviation from s = se × √n: 1.2 × 10 = 12 and 0.6 × 20 = 12. The spread of individual commutes is the same.

options.text: Survey A's mean is more precise, because its standard error is larger.
options.feedback: A larger standard error means less precision: the sample mean varies more from sample to sample.

options.text: Survey B's mean is the more precise estimate of the city's mean commute.
options.feedback: Correct. Its standard error is half as large, because it uses four times as many commuters.

options.text: Survey B's sample mean must be closer to the true mean than Survey A's.
options.feedback: Precision describes how much a sample mean varies across samples; any single sample mean can still miss by more or less.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 4.1: a smaller standard error means a more precise estimate. Both surveys have a standard deviation of about 12 minutes; Survey B is more precise only because n is four times larger.

practice.concept: Standard error and precision (Section 4.1, Key Concept 4.1)
practice.stem: Doubling the sample size divides the standard error of the mean by about 1.41 (that is, √2), not by 2.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. se = s/√n, so doubling n multiplies the denominator by √2 ≈ 1.41.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit how the standard error depends on n: it uses the square root of the sample size (Key Concept 4.1).

practice.explanation: Key Concept 4.1: the standard error falls at rate 1/√n. Doubling n divides it by √2 ≈ 1.41; quadrupling n halves it.

practice.stem: Figure 4.1 compares the t-distribution with 4 degrees of freedom, t(4), with the standard normal. How does t(4) differ from the standard normal?

options.text: It is skewed to the right, with a longer upper tail than the normal.
options.feedback: The t-distribution is symmetric around zero, just like the standard normal.

options.text: It is narrower than the normal, with thinner tails and fewer extremes.
options.feedback: The t-distribution has more probability in the tails, not less.

options.text: It is symmetric around zero, with fatter tails than the normal.
options.feedback: Correct. Fatter tails reflect the extra uncertainty from estimating σ with s.

options.text: It is identical to the normal, because both are bell-shaped.
options.feedback: With only 4 degrees of freedom, the t-distribution is visibly different: more probability sits in its tails.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 4.2: the t-distribution is symmetric around zero like N(0,1), but its tails are fatter, especially with few degrees of freedom.

practice.stem: A sample has n = 10 observations. What is the critical value for a two-sided 95% confidence interval for the mean (Practice Exercise 3)?

options.feedback: Correct. With n − 1 = 9 degrees of freedom, \( t_{9,\,0.025} \approx 2.262 \).
1.96 is the standard normal value. With only 9 degrees of freedom, the t critical value is noticeably larger.
This is the value for 10 degrees of freedom. The t-statistic for a mean has n − 1 degrees of freedom.
This leaves 5% in one tail. A two-sided 95% interval leaves 2.5% in each tail.

practice.explanation: For a 95% interval use \( t_{n-1,\,0.025} \). With n = 10 that is \( t_{9,\,0.025} \approx 2.262 \), well above 1.96 because t(9) has fat tails.

practice.stem: With n = 100, the two-sided 95% t critical value is far above 1.96, so the normal distribution is a poor approximation.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Look up \( t_{99,\,0.025} \) and compare it with 1.96 (Section 4.2).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. \( t_{99,\,0.025} \approx 1.98 \), very close to 1.96: with many degrees of freedom, t is nearly normal.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 4.2: as n grows, the t-distribution approaches the standard normal. With 99 degrees of freedom the critical value is about 1.98, almost 1.96.

practice.stem: A 95% confidence interval for mean household income is [$48,000, $56,000] (Practice Exercise 1). What are the point estimate and the margin of error?

options.text: Point estimate $52,000; margin of error $8,000
options.feedback: $8,000 is the full width of the interval. The margin of error is the distance from the center to either end.

options.text: Point estimate $52,000; margin of error $4,000
options.feedback: Correct. The interval is centered on the estimate: (48,000 + 56,000)/2 = $52,000, and each end is $4,000 away.

options.text: Point estimate $48,000; margin of error $4,000
options.feedback: $48,000 is the lower end. The point estimate sits at the center of the interval.

options.text: Point estimate $56,000; margin of error $8,000
options.feedback: $56,000 is the upper end, and $8,000 is the full width.

practice.explanation: An interval estimate ± margin of error is centered on the estimate: midpoint $52,000, margin of error (56,000 − 48,000)/2 = $4,000.

practice.stem: Suppose a large-sample 90% confidence interval for mean commute time is [27, 33] minutes. From the same data, what would the 95% interval be, approximately? (Use the normal critical values 1.645 and 1.96.)

options.text: [27, 33], because the data have not changed
options.feedback: The data are the same, but the critical value changes with the confidence level, so the margin of error changes too.
This scales the margin by 1.645/1.96, which shrinks it. Higher confidence calls for a larger multiplier.

options.text: It cannot be found without the raw data
options.feedback: The interval gives the center (30) and the margin (3 = 1.645 × se), which is enough to recover se.
Correct. se = 3/1.645 ≈ 1.82, so the 95% margin is 1.96 × 1.82 ≈ 3.6 minutes around 30.

practice.explanation: Higher confidence requires a larger critical value, hence a wider interval: margin = 3 × 1.96/1.645 ≈ 3.6, giving about [26.4, 33.6].

practice.stem: A 95% confidence interval for mean household income is [$48,000, $56,000]. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: There is a 95% probability that the population mean lies in this particular interval.
options.feedback: The chapter lists this as a common misinterpretation: μ is fixed, and the 95% describes the procedure across repeated samples.

options.text: If the sampling were repeated many times, about 95% of the intervals built this way would contain μ.
options.feedback: Correct: this is the repeated-sampling meaning of 95% confidence.

options.text: With a sample four times as large, the interval would keep the same width.
options.feedback: Quadrupling n halves the standard error, so the interval would be about half as wide.

options.text: A two-sided test at α = 0.05 would not reject H₀: μ = $50,000.
options.feedback: Correct: $50,000 lies inside the 95% interval, and values inside it are not rejected at the 5% level.

options.text: A 99% interval from the same data would be narrower.
options.feedback: Higher confidence requires a larger critical value, so the 99% interval would be wider.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 4.3: 95% describes how often the procedure captures μ in repeated samples. Values inside a 95% interval are not rejected by a two-sided test at α = 0.05 (Section 4.4).

practice.stem: Suppose a sample of 64 workers has a mean wage of $45,000 and a standard error of $2,000. Using the rule of thumb 'mean ± 2 × SE', what is the approximate 95% confidence interval?

options.feedback: This adds and subtracts only one standard error, which gives roughly a 68% interval.
This uses two standard deviations ($16,000) instead of two standard errors. That range describes individual wages, not the mean.
This uses one standard deviation ($16,000) instead of standard errors.

practice.stem: Suppose two surveys of the same population use n = 100 and n = 400. The 95% confidence interval from the larger survey will typically be about half as wide.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. Quadrupling n halves the standard error, and the interval width is proportional to the standard error.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit how the interval width depends on the standard error, and how the standard error depends on n (Sections 4.1 and 4.3).

practice.explanation: Width = 2 × critical value × se, and se = s/√n. Going from n = 100 to n = 400 doubles √n, so the width roughly halves (the critical value barely changes).

practice.stem: Test H₀: μ = 100 against Hₐ: μ ≠ 100 with a sample mean of 105, a standard error of 3, and n = 49 (Practice Exercise 4). What is the t-statistic?

options.feedback: 5 is the difference between the sample mean and the hypothesized value. The t-statistic measures it in standard errors.
This divides the sample mean by the standard error. The t-statistic starts from the distance to the hypothesized value.
This divides the difference by √49 = 7. The standard error (3) is already given; divide by it.

practice.explanation: t = (x̄ − μ₀)/se(x̄) = (105 − 100)/3 ≈ 1.67: the sample mean is 1.67 standard errors above the hypothesized value.

practice.stem: Continuing the example: t ≈ 1.67 with n = 49, and the two-sided 5% critical value is about 2.01. What is the decision at α = 0.05?

options.text: Reject H₀, because the t-statistic of 1.67 is a positive number.
options.feedback: The sign shows the direction of the gap; the decision depends on how large |t| is compared with the critical value.

options.text: Reject H₀, because 1.67 exceeds the critical value of 1.645.
options.feedback: 1.645 is a one-sided normal critical value. A two-sided 5% test puts 2.5% in each tail.

options.text: Do not reject H₀, because |t| is below the critical value of 2.01.
options.feedback: Correct. 1.67 < 2.01, so the result is not significant at 5% (the p-value is about 0.10).

options.text: Do not reject H₀, because the p-value is below 0.05.
options.feedback: A p-value below α would lead to rejection, not the reverse. Here the p-value is about 0.10.

practice.explanation: Critical-value approach: reject if |t| > \( t_{48,\,0.025} \approx 2.01 \). Since 1.67 < 2.01, do not reject; equivalently, p ≈ 0.10 > 0.05.

practice.stem: A two-sided test gives a p-value of 0.03. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: H₀ is rejected at α = 0.05.
options.feedback: Correct: 0.03 < 0.05.

options.text: If H₀ were true, a result at least this extreme would occur in about 3% of samples.
options.feedback: Correct: this is the definition of the p-value.

options.text: There is a 3% probability that H₀ is true.
options.feedback: A p-value is computed assuming H₀ is true; it is not the probability that H₀ is true.

options.text: H₀ is not rejected at α = 0.01.
options.feedback: Correct: 0.03 > 0.01, so the stricter test does not reject.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 4.4: the p-value is the probability, if H₀ were true, of a result at least as extreme as ours. Reject when p < α: here at 5% but not at 1%.

practice.stem: A sample has n = 36, mean 72, and standard deviation 18. Test H₀: μ = 75 against Hₐ: μ ≠ 75 at α = 0.05 (Practice Exercise 5). The two-sided critical value is about 2.03. What is the decision?

options.text: Reject H₀, because the sample mean of 72 is below 75.
options.feedback: Any sample mean differs a little from 75; the question is whether the gap is large relative to the standard error.

options.text: Do not reject H₀, because |t| = 1.00 is below the critical value.
Reject H₀, because t is negative and so it lies in the lower rejection region.
options.feedback: The lower rejection region starts at −2.03. A t of −1.00 is negative but far from that cutoff.

options.text: No decision is possible without the population standard deviation.
options.feedback: The t-test exists precisely for this case: it uses the sample standard deviation s.

practice.explanation: se = 18/√36 = 3 and t = (72 − 75)/3 = −1.00. Reject only if |t| > 2.03, so H₀ is not rejected (two-sided p ≈ 0.32).

practice.stem: A p-value of 0.30 means there is a 30% probability that the null hypothesis is true.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit what the p-value conditions on: it is computed assuming H₀ is true (Key Concept 4.4).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. The p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme as ours if H₀ were true, not the probability that H₀ is true.

practice.explanation: Common mistake (Key Takeaways): a p-value is NOT the probability that H₀ is true. It measures how surprising the data would be if H₀ were true.

practice.concept: Type I and Type II errors (Section 4.4)
practice.stem: A clinical trial tests H₀: a new drug has no effect. Which outcome is a Type II error?

options.text: The trial concludes the drug works, when in fact it has no effect.
options.feedback: Rejecting a true H₀ is a Type I error (a false alarm).

options.text: The trial concludes the drug works, and in fact it does work.
options.feedback: Rejecting a false H₀ is a correct decision; its probability is the test's power.

options.text: The trial finds no evidence of an effect, and in fact there is none.
options.feedback: Not rejecting a true H₀ is a correct decision.

options.text: The trial finds no evidence of an effect, when in fact the drug works.
options.feedback: Correct. Failing to reject a false H₀ is a Type II error (a missed effect).

practice.explanation: Type I error: reject a true H₀ (probability α). Type II error: fail to reject a false H₀ (probability β). Power = 1 − β.

practice.stem: Suppose a test of H₀: μ = 100 uses n = 50 and α = 0.05. If H₀ is false, for which true mean is the test's power highest?

options.feedback: A true mean close to 100 is hard to tell apart from the null value, so power is low.
This is still close to 100. Power grows as the true mean moves farther from the hypothesized value.
This difference is the smallest of all, so it is the hardest to detect.
Correct. The farther the true mean is from 100, the easier the difference is to detect.

practice.explanation: Section 4.4: larger effects are easier to detect. With the same n and α, power is highest when the true mean is farthest from the hypothesized value.

practice.stem: Suppose a researcher raises α from 0.05 to 0.10 for a two-sided test, with the same sample size. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The probability of a Type I error falls.
options.feedback: α is the probability of a Type I error, so raising α raises it.

options.text: A smaller |t| is now enough to reject H₀.
options.feedback: Correct: a larger α moves the critical value closer to zero.

options.text: The probability of a Type II error falls.
options.feedback: Correct: rejecting more easily means missing fewer real effects.

options.text: The test's power rises.
options.feedback: Correct: power = 1 − β rises when β falls.

options.text: The test now rejects H₀ only when the p-value is below 0.05.
options.feedback: The decision rule compares p with the new α: reject when p < 0.10.

practice.explanation: Section 4.4: raising α moves the critical value toward zero (rejection when p < 0.10), trading a higher Type I error rate for a lower Type II error rate and higher power. Reducing both errors at once requires a larger sample.

practice.concept: Statistical and practical significance (Section 4.5, Key Concept 4.5)
practice.stem: Suppose a national survey of 1,000,000 workers finds mean weekly hours of 40.02, and a test of H₀: μ = 40 gives p < 0.001. What is the best reading?

options.text: Workers put in far more than 40 hours a week, an economically large gap.
options.feedback: The gap is 0.02 hours, about a minute a week. A small p-value does not make a difference large.

options.text: The result proves that every worker in the country works more than 40 hours a week.
options.feedback: A test is about the mean, not about every individual; many workers surely work fewer hours.

options.text: The gap is significant but trivial in size: about a minute a week.
options.feedback: Correct. A huge sample detects a tiny difference; whether it matters is a separate question.

options.text: There is a 99.9% probability that mean hours exceed 40.
options.feedback: A p-value is not a probability about μ; it describes how unusual the data would be if H₀ were true.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 4.5: statistical significance asks 'Is there a difference?'; practical significance asks 'Does it matter?'. With n = 1,000,000, a 0.02-hour gap (about 1.2 minutes) is detectable but economically trivial.

practice.concept: Statistical and practical significance (Section 4.5, Key Concept 4.5)
practice.stem: Suppose two studies each find a $5 gap between the sample mean and the hypothesized value. Study A has a standard error of $1; Study B has a standard error of $10. Which statement is correct?

options.text: A's t is 5 and B's is 0.5: only A's gap is many standard errors from H₀.
options.feedback: Correct. The t-statistic measures the gap in standard errors, so precision decides.

options.text: Both results are equally significant, because the dollar gap is the same.
options.feedback: Significance depends on the gap relative to its standard error, which differs tenfold here.

options.text: B is more significant, because a larger standard error means more variation was detected.
options.feedback: A larger standard error means less precision, which makes significance harder to reach.

options.text: Neither can be significant, because a $5 gap is economically small.
options.feedback: Statistical significance does not depend on whether a gap feels large; it depends on the standard error.

practice.explanation: t = gap/se: 5/1 = 5 for Study A and 5/10 = 0.5 for Study B. The same dollar gap can be highly significant or not at all, depending on precision (Key Concept 4.5).

practice.stem: Suppose a test of whether mean apartment rent in a town equals $1,200 gives a two-sided p-value of 0.40. Which wording of the result is best?

options.text: We accept H₀: the town's mean apartment rent is therefore exactly $1,200.
options.feedback: Failing to reject is not the same as accepting: other values near $1,200 fit the data too (Key Concept 4.6).

options.text: The data give little evidence against $1,200, but nearby rents fit them too.
options.feedback: Correct. A large p-value means weak evidence against H₀, not proof of it.

options.text: We should switch to a one-sided test to get a smaller p-value.
options.feedback: Choosing the test after seeing the data is p-hacking; the choice must be made in advance (Section 4.6).

options.text: The sample must have been too small, so the result should be ignored.
options.feedback: A non-significant result is still informative; a confidence interval shows which values remain plausible.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 4.6: 'fail to reject' does not mean 'accept'. The data are consistent with H₀, but the test may lack power, and a confidence interval shows the full range of plausible values.

practice.concept: Statistical and practical significance (Section 4.5, Key Concept 4.5)
practice.stem: Suppose a city tests whether its mean commute differs from the national 27 minutes. With n = 400, the sample mean is 27.5 minutes, se = 0.25, t = 2.0, and p ≈ 0.046. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The difference is statistically significant at α = 0.01.
options.feedback: 0.046 is above 0.01, so the stricter test does not reject.

options.text: The difference is statistically significant at α = 0.05.
options.feedback: Correct: 0.046 < 0.05.

options.text: Whether an extra 30 seconds matters is a separate economic question.
options.feedback: Correct: statistical significance says the gap is unlikely to be chance, not that it is important.

options.text: Because p < 0.05, the city's commutes are much longer than the national average.
options.feedback: The p-value does not measure size: the estimated gap is only half a minute.

practice.explanation: Key Concepts 4.5 and 4.7: a result can be significant at 5% (not at 1%) and still small in economic terms; context decides whether 30 seconds matters.

practice.stem: A sample has n = 36, mean 72, and standard deviation 18, so t = −1.00, and the two-sided p-value for H₀: μ = 75 is about 0.32. What is the p-value for the lower-tailed test H₀: μ ≥ 75 against Hₐ: μ < 75?

options.text: About 0.32
options.feedback: A one-sided test counts only one tail, so its p-value differs from the two-sided one.

options.text: About 0.16
options.feedback: Correct. The sample mean is below 75, the direction of Hₐ, so the one-sided p-value is half the two-sided one.

options.text: About 0.84
options.feedback: This is the upper-tail probability Pr[T ≥ −1]. A lower-tailed test uses Pr[T ≤ t].

options.text: About 0.64
options.feedback: This doubles the two-sided p-value. A one-sided test uses one tail, so the p-value gets smaller, not larger.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 4.8: for a lower-tailed test, p = Pr[T ≤ t] = Pr[T ≤ −1.00] ≈ 0.16, half the two-sided p-value of 0.32 because the effect is in the predicted direction.

practice.stem: When is a one-sided test appropriate? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: When theory predicts the direction of the effect before the data are seen.
options.feedback: Correct: the chapter recommends one-sided tests when theory specifies a direction.

options.text: When the question is directional, such as whether a policy increases income.
options.feedback: Correct: a directional claim calls for a directional alternative.

options.text: When a two-sided test gave p = 0.08 and a one-sided test would give p = 0.04.
options.feedback: Switching after seeing the data is p-hacking; the choice must be made in advance.

options.text: When effects in either direction would be interesting.
options.feedback: If both directions matter, a two-sided test is the right choice.

options.text: When a drug is tested only for being better than a placebo, decided in advance.
options.feedback: Correct: 'better than' is a directional claim, chosen before the data.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 4.8: use one-sided tests when theory or the question specifies a direction, chosen before seeing the data. Choosing them after a two-sided test fails is p-hacking.

practice.stem: In a lower-tailed test (H₀: μ ≥ μ* against Hₐ: μ < μ*), the p-value is the probability in the lower tail, Pr[T ≤ t].

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. A lower-tailed test looks for evidence that μ is smaller than μ*, so it counts only the lower tail.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit Section 4.6: which tail matches the direction of the alternative hypothesis?

practice.explanation: Section 4.6: upper-tailed tests use p = Pr[T ≥ t]; lower-tailed tests use p = Pr[T ≤ t].

practice.stem: In a survey of 500 people, 275 support a policy, so p̂ = 0.55 and se(p̂) ≈ 0.022 (Practice Exercise 7). What is the 95% confidence interval for the population proportion?

options.feedback: This adds and subtracts one standard error. A 95% interval uses the critical value 1.96.
This centers the interval on 0.50 instead of on the sample proportion.
This uses 2.576, the 99% critical value.

practice.stem: In the same survey (275 of 500, p̂ = 0.55), a test of H₀: p = 0.50 gives z ≈ 2.24 and a two-sided p-value of about 0.025. What is the conclusion at α = 0.05?

options.text: Reject H₀, because |z| ≈ 2.24 exceeds 1.96.
options.feedback: Correct. 2.24 > 1.96, equivalently p ≈ 0.025 < 0.05.

options.text: Do not reject H₀, because 0.55 is close to the hypothesized 0.50.
options.feedback: Closeness must be judged in standard errors: 0.05 is more than two standard errors here.

options.text: Reject H₀ simply because 275 is more than half of 500.
options.feedback: Any sample can land above half by chance; the test asks whether the gap is large relative to its standard error.

options.text: Do not reject H₀, because the p-value of 0.025 is above α.
options.feedback: Compare again: 0.025 is below 0.05.

practice.stem: With p̂ = 0.55 held fixed, a test of H₀: p = 0.50 gives the same z-statistic whether the sample has 500 or 5,000 people.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit how the standard error of a proportion depends on n (Section 4.7).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. The standard error shrinks with √n, so the same 5-point gap is more standard errors from 0.50 in the larger sample (z ≈ 7.1 instead of 2.24).

practice.explanation: Section 4.7: se = √(p(1 − p)/n) falls as n grows, so the same sample proportion produces a larger z in a larger sample, just as in the chapter's 2,500-voter example.

exam.concept: Standard error and precision (Section 4.1, Key Concept 4.1)
exam.stem: For the sample of 171 women, the chapter reports both the standard deviation of earnings and the standard error of the mean. What does the standard error measure?

options.text: How much individual women's earnings typically differ from the sample mean.
options.feedback: Revisit the difference between variation among individuals and variation of a statistic (Section 4.1).

options.text: The share of women whose earnings lie within one standard error of the mean.
options.feedback: Revisit what the standard error describes: a share of people, or something else? (Key Concept 4.1)

options.text: How much the sample mean would typically vary across samples of 171 women.
options.feedback: Correct. The standard error measures the precision of x̄ as an estimate of μ.

options.text: The exact gap between this sample's mean and the true population mean.
options.feedback: The true mean is unknown, so its exact gap from x̄ cannot be computed. Revisit Key Concept 4.1.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 4.1: the standard deviation ($25,527) describes how individual earnings vary; the standard error ($1,952) describes how the sample mean would vary across repeated samples of 171 women.

exam.concept: Standard error and precision (Section 4.1, Key Concept 4.1)
exam.stem: Suppose the earnings sample were enlarged from 171 to 684 women (four times as many), with about the same standard deviation. What would happen to the standard error of the mean?

options.text: It would be cut in half.
options.feedback: Correct. se = s/√n, and √4 = 2.

options.text: It would fall to one-quarter of its size.
options.feedback: Check how the standard error depends on n in the formula of Key Concept 4.1.

options.text: It would double.
options.feedback: Revisit whether more data make the sample mean more or less precise (Section 4.1).

options.text: It would not change, because the standard deviation stays the same.
options.feedback: Look at the formula in Key Concept 4.1: the standard deviation is not the only ingredient.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 4.1: se = s/√n falls at rate 1/√n. Quadrupling the sample halves the standard error, from $1,952 to about $976.

exam.concept: Standard error and precision (Section 4.1, Key Concept 4.1)
exam.stem: For the 191 men, the standard deviation of earnings is about $65,035 and the mean is $52,354. What is the standard error of the mean?

options.text: About $4,706
About $340
options.feedback: Revisit how the standard error is computed (Key Concept 4.1).

options.text: About $3,788
options.feedback: Revisit how the standard error is computed (Key Concept 4.1).

options.text: About $65,035
options.feedback: Revisit how the standard error is computed (Key Concept 4.1).

exam.explanation: se(x̄) = s/√n = 65,035/√191 ≈ $4,706, about 14 times smaller than the standard deviation because √191 ≈ 13.8.

exam.concept: Standard error and precision (Section 4.1, Key Concept 4.1)
exam.stem: Collecting a larger sample of 30-year-old women would be expected to shrink the standard deviation of their earnings in the same proportion as the standard error.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit what each measure describes: individuals or the sample mean (Section 4.1).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. The standard deviation describes the spread of individual earnings in the population, which more data do not reduce; only the standard error falls with n.

exam.explanation: Section 4.1: the standard deviation ($25,527) measures variability among women and stays roughly the same as n grows; the standard error s/√n shrinks.

exam.stem: Why does the chapter use the t-distribution, rather than the standard normal, for inference about mean earnings?

options.text: Because earnings are right-skewed, and the t-distribution is designed for skewed data.
options.feedback: Revisit the shape of the t-distribution and the reason Section 4.2 gives for using it.

options.text: Because a sample of 171 women is too small for the sample mean to be computed reliably.
options.feedback: The sample mean can be computed for any sample. Revisit the reason given in Key Concept 4.2.

options.text: Because the t-distribution allows the interval to be centered on the median, not the mean.
options.feedback: Intervals for μ are centered on the sample mean. Revisit Key Concept 4.2.

options.text: Because the population standard deviation is unknown and is estimated by s from the sample.
options.feedback: Correct. Estimating σ with s adds uncertainty, which the t-distribution accounts for.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 4.2: the t-distribution is used when σ is unknown and estimated by s. The extra uncertainty gives it fatter tails than N(0,1).

exam.stem: The gas-price test uses 32 stations and estimates the standard deviation from the sample. Under H₀, which distribution does the chapter use for the t-statistic?

options.text: The standard normal, because the sample has more than 30 stations
options.feedback: Revisit the distribution of the t-statistic for a mean in Section 4.2.

options.text: The t-distribution with 31 degrees of freedom
options.feedback: Correct. The t-statistic for a mean follows T(n − 1) = T(31).

options.text: The t-distribution with 32 degrees of freedom
options.feedback: Revisit the distribution of the t-statistic for a mean in Section 4.2.

options.text: A normal distribution whose spread equals the sample standard deviation of prices
options.feedback: Revisit the distribution of the t-statistic for a mean in Section 4.2.

exam.explanation: Section 4.2: t = (x̄ − μ)/se(x̄) ~ T(n − 1). With 32 stations, n − 1 = 31, which gives the critical value ±2.04 used in the test.

exam.stem: Because the t-distribution has fatter tails than the standard normal, a 95% interval built with a t critical value is wider than one built with 1.96, for the same standard error.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. Fatter tails push the 2.5% cutoffs farther out, so \( t_{n-1,\,0.025} \) exceeds 1.96 (for example 2.04 with 31 degrees of freedom).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit how fat tails affect where the 2.5% cutoffs lie (Key Concept 4.2).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 4.2: with fat tails, more probability lies far from zero, so the 95% cutoffs are larger than 1.96 (1.974 for 170 degrees of freedom, 2.04 for 31).

exam.stem: The 95% confidence interval for the mean earnings of 30-year-old women working full-time is [$37,559, $45,266]. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: About 95% of 30-year-old women working full-time earn between $37,559 and $45,266.
options.feedback: Revisit whether the interval describes individual women or a population parameter (Section 4.3).

options.text: There is a 95% probability that μ lies in this particular interval of $37,559 to $45,266.
options.feedback: Revisit what is fixed and what is random in a confidence interval (Section 4.3).

options.text: About 95% of sample means from repeated samples would fall between $37,559 and $45,266.
options.feedback: Revisit what the 95% refers to across repeated samples (Key Concept 4.3).

options.text: Across repeated samples of 171, about 95% of intervals built this way would contain μ.
options.feedback: Correct. The 95% describes how often the procedure captures the fixed μ.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 4.3: μ is fixed and the interval is random. About 95% of intervals built this way from repeated samples of 171 women would contain μ; this one is our best range of plausible values.

exam.stem: Using the same data, an analyst switches from a 95% to a 99% confidence interval for mean earnings. What happens to the interval?

options.text: It becomes narrower, because higher confidence means a more precise estimate.
options.feedback: Revisit the confidence–precision trade-off in Section 4.3.

options.text: It keeps the same width, because the data and the standard error have not changed.
options.feedback: Revisit the confidence–precision trade-off in Section 4.3.

options.text: It becomes wider, because a higher confidence level requires a larger critical value.
options.feedback: Correct. The multiplier rises (from about 1.97 to about 2.61), so the interval widens.

options.text: It becomes wider, because the standard error is larger at the 99% confidence level.
options.feedback: Revisit the confidence–precision trade-off in Section 4.3.

exam.explanation: Section 4.3: higher confidence requires a larger critical value. For the women, the 95% interval is $7,707 wide and the 99% interval $10,171 wide; the standard error ($1,952) is the same.

exam.stem: The 95% confidence interval for mean earnings is [$37,559, $45,266]. Which hypothesized values of μ would a two-sided test at α = 0.05 reject? (Select all that apply.)

options.feedback: Correct: $36,000 lies outside the 95% interval (t ≈ 2.77).
Revisit how a 95% interval relates to two-sided tests at the 5% level (Section 4.4).
Revisit how a 95% interval relates to two-sided tests at the 5% level (Section 4.4).
Correct: $46,500 lies above the interval's upper end (t ≈ −2.61).

exam.explanation: Section 4.4: values outside the 95% interval are rejected at α = 0.05 (two-sided) and values inside are not. $36,000 and $46,500 are outside; $38,000 and $44,000 are inside.

exam.stem: For the 32 Yolo County gas stations, the mean price is $3.67 per gallon and the standard error is $0.027. Using the rule of thumb 'mean ± 2 × SE', what is the approximate 95% confidence interval?

options.feedback: Revisit the rule of thumb for a 95% interval in Section 4.3.
Revisit the rule of thumb for a 95% interval in Section 4.3.
Revisit the rule of thumb for a 95% interval in Section 4.3.

exam.explanation: For n > 30, the 95% interval is about x̄ ± 2 × se = 3.67 ± 0.054 ≈ [$3.62, $3.72]. It does not contain the state average of $3.81.

exam.stem: Suppose two samples of women have the same size and the same standard deviation of earnings, but different sample means. Their 95% confidence intervals for mean earnings have the same width.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. Width = 2 × critical value × se, and se = s/√n is the same for both; the sample mean only sets the center.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit the formula x̄ ± t × se(x̄): which parts set the center, and which set the width? (Section 4.3)

exam.explanation: Section 4.3: the interval x̄ ± \( t_{n-1,\,0.025} \) × se(x̄) is centered on x̄. With equal n and equal s, both samples have the same se and critical value, so the intervals have the same width 2 × t × se, just at different centers.

exam.stem: To test H₀: μ = $40,000 for the women, the chapter uses the sample mean ($41,413), the standard deviation ($25,527), and the standard error ($1,952). What is the t-statistic?

options.text: About 0.06
options.feedback: Revisit how the t-statistic is built in Section 4.4.

options.text: About 0.72
About 8.26
options.feedback: Check the denominator of the t-statistic in Section 4.4.

options.text: About 21.22
options.feedback: Check the numerator of the t-statistic in Section 4.4.

exam.explanation: t = (x̄ − μ₀)/se(x̄) = (41,413 − 40,000)/1,952 ≈ 0.72: the sample mean is less than one standard error above $40,000.

exam.stem: The two-sided test of H₀: μ = $40,000 for the women's earnings gives p = 0.47. Which statement is correct?

options.text: If μ = $40,000, about 47% of samples would give a mean at least this far from $40,000.
options.feedback: Correct. This is the definition of the p-value.

options.text: There is a 47% probability that the null hypothesis μ = $40,000 is true.
options.feedback: Revisit what the p-value assumes and what it measures (Key Concept 4.4).

options.text: About 47% of 30-year-old women working full-time earn more than $40,000.
options.feedback: Revisit whether a p-value describes individual women or a test statistic (Section 4.4).

options.text: The test shows that mean earnings equal $40,000, because the p-value is well above 0.05.
options.feedback: Revisit what a large p-value can and cannot establish (Key Concept 4.6).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 4.4: the p-value is the probability, if H₀ were true, of a result at least as extreme as ours. p = 0.47 > 0.05, so H₀ is not rejected; that does not prove μ = $40,000.

exam.stem: Which statements about two-sided hypothesis tests at α = 0.05 are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: H₀ is rejected when the p-value is above α, the chosen significance level.
options.feedback: Revisit the p-value decision rule in Section 4.4.

options.text: The p-value approach and the critical-value approach always reach the same decision.
options.feedback: Correct: the chapter notes that both methods always give the same conclusion.

options.text: A larger |t| goes with a larger p-value.
options.feedback: Revisit how the p-value is computed from the tails beyond |t| (Section 4.4).

options.text: The 5% rejection probability is split between both tails, 2.5% in each.
options.feedback: Correct: a two-sided test puts α/2 in each tail.

exam.explanation: Section 4.4: reject H₀ if p < α or, equivalently, if |t| > \( t_{n-1,\,\alpha/2} \). The two rules always agree, and a larger |t| means a smaller p-value.

exam.stem: In the gas-price test of H₀: μ = $3.81 (n = 32), t = −5.26 and the two-sided 5% critical value is ±2.04. What is the decision?

options.text: Do not reject H₀, because only positive t-statistics can fall in the rejection region.
options.feedback: Revisit where the rejection regions lie in a two-sided test (Section 4.4).

options.text: Do not reject H₀, because −5.26 is smaller than the critical value of 2.04.
options.feedback: Revisit how t is compared with the critical value in a two-sided test (Section 4.4).

options.text: Reject H₀, because any nonzero t-statistic signals a real difference.
options.feedback: Revisit the decision rules in Section 4.4.

options.text: Reject H₀, because |t| = 5.26 exceeds 2.04; prices are below the state average.
options.feedback: Correct. |t| is far beyond the critical value, and the negative sign means prices are lower.

exam.explanation: Reject H₀ if |t| > 2.04. Here |−5.26| = 5.26, so H₀ is rejected (p < 0.0001); the negative t shows Yolo County prices are below $3.81.

exam.stem: If a two-sided test rejects H₀ at α = 0.01, then the same test with the same data also rejects H₀ at α = 0.05.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. Rejecting at 1% means p < 0.01, which is also below 0.05.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Compare the p-value needed to reject at α = 0.01 with the threshold at α = 0.05 (Section 4.4).

exam.explanation: Reject when p < α. A p-value below 0.01 is automatically below 0.05, so rejection at a stricter level implies rejection at a looser one (but not the reverse).

exam.concept: Type I and Type II errors (Section 4.4)
exam.stem: In the test of H₀: μ = $40,000 for women's mean earnings, which outcome would be a Type I error?

options.text: Not rejecting H₀ when true mean earnings actually differ from $40,000
options.feedback: Revisit the four possible outcomes of a test in Section 4.4.

options.text: Not rejecting H₀ when true mean earnings actually equal $40,000
options.feedback: Revisit the four possible outcomes of a test in Section 4.4.

options.text: Rejecting H₀ when true mean earnings actually differ from $40,000
options.feedback: Revisit the four possible outcomes of a test in Section 4.4.

options.text: Rejecting H₀ when true mean earnings actually equal $40,000
options.feedback: Correct. A Type I error is rejecting a true null hypothesis (a false alarm).

exam.explanation: Section 4.4: a Type I error rejects a true H₀ (probability α); a Type II error fails to reject a false H₀. Here a Type I error would be concluding μ ≠ $40,000 when μ = $40,000.

exam.stem: Suppose the true mean earnings of all such women are $41,400, so H₀: μ = $40,000 is false. Which change would most raise the chance that the test detects this, without raising the Type I error rate?

options.text: Collect a smaller sample, so that each woman's earnings carry more weight.
options.feedback: Revisit how the sample size affects the standard error and the power of a test (Section 4.4).

options.text: Collect a larger sample of women from the same population.
options.feedback: Correct. A larger n shrinks the standard error, so the same gap produces a larger |t|.

options.text: Test H₀: μ = $41,400 instead, since it is closer to the sample mean.
options.feedback: Changing the hypothesis changes the question being asked; revisit what power refers to (Section 4.4).

options.text: Report 'accept H₀' instead of 'fail to reject H₀', which removes the Type II error.
options.feedback: Wording does not change what the test can detect. Revisit Key Concept 4.6 and Section 4.4.

exam.explanation: Section 4.4: a larger sample shrinks se = s/√n, which raises power without changing α. With n = 684 the standard error would halve, though even then a $1,413 gap gives t of only about 1.45.

exam.concept: Type I and Type II errors (Section 4.4)
exam.stem: Suppose the analyst lowers α from 0.05 to 0.01 for the earnings test, with the same sample size. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The probability of a Type I error falls.
options.feedback: Correct: α is the probability of a Type I error.

options.text: The probability of a Type II error rises.
options.feedback: Correct: a stricter cutoff misses more real effects.

options.text: Stronger evidence (a larger |t|) is needed to reject H₀.
options.feedback: Correct: a smaller α moves the critical value farther from zero.

options.text: The power of the test, the chance of rejecting a false H₀, rises.
options.feedback: Revisit the trade-off between the two types of error in Section 4.4.

exam.explanation: Section 4.4: decreasing α lowers the Type I error rate but raises the Type II error rate and lowers power. Only a larger sample improves power without raising α.

exam.concept: Statistical and practical significance (Section 4.5, Key Concept 4.5)
exam.stem: Yolo County gas prices average about $0.14 per gallon below the $3.81 state average, and the test gives p < 0.0001. Which statement best separates statistical from practical significance?

options.text: The gap is unlikely to be due to chance; whether 14 cents matters is a separate question.
options.feedback: Correct. Statistical significance and economic importance are different questions.

options.text: Because p < 0.0001, the price gap must be economically large for every driver.
options.feedback: Revisit what a p-value says about the size of a difference (Key Concept 4.5).

options.text: Because 14 cents is a small amount, the gap cannot be statistically significant.
options.feedback: Revisit what drives statistical significance besides the size of the gap (Key Concept 4.5).

options.text: The p-value measures the size of the gap: a smaller p means a bigger difference in dollars.
options.feedback: Revisit what the p-value measures (Section 4.4) and what practical significance asks (Key Concept 4.5).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 4.5: 'Is there a difference?' (statistical) and 'Does it matter?' (practical) are separate. The chapter judges 14 cents meaningful: about $2.10 per 15-gallon tank, or about $109 a year.

exam.concept: Statistical and practical significance (Section 4.5, Key Concept 4.5)
exam.stem: The gas-price gap is only $0.14, yet t = −5.26. The women's earnings gap from $40,000 is $1,413, yet that test is far from significant. What explains the contrast?

options.text: Gas is bought every week, so small price gaps count more in a t-test than earnings gaps.
options.feedback: Revisit what goes into the t-statistic (Section 4.4).

options.text: Each gap is judged against its own standard error: $0.027 for gas and $1,952 for earnings.
options.feedback: Correct. $0.14 is over five standard errors; $1,413 is less than one.

options.text: The earnings sample is larger, and larger samples make significance harder to reach.
options.feedback: Revisit how the sample size affects the standard error (Key Concept 4.1).

options.text: Gas prices are recorded in cents, which multiplies the t-statistic by 100.
options.feedback: Revisit whether the units of measurement affect a t-statistic (Section 4.4).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 4.5: t = gap ÷ standard error. Gas prices vary little across stations, so se = $0.027 and the $0.14 gap is 5.26 standard errors; earnings vary a lot, so se = $1,952 and $1,413 is about 0.72 standard errors.

exam.stem: For 191 men, the sample mean of earnings is $52,354, and the two-sided test of H₀: μ = $50,000 gives p = 0.62. Which conclusion is appropriate?

options.text: Men's mean earnings in the population equal $50,000.
options.feedback: Revisit what a test can establish when it does not reject (Key Concept 4.6).

options.text: Men earn more than $50,000 on average, because $52,354 is above $50,000.
options.feedback: Revisit how a test judges a gap between the sample mean and the hypothesized value (Section 4.4).

options.text: We fail to reject H₀, so $50,000 remains one of many plausible values.
options.feedback: Correct. Not rejecting H₀ is not the same as proving it.

options.text: There is about a 62% probability that men's mean earnings equal $50,000.
options.feedback: Revisit what a p-value measures (Key Concept 4.4).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 4.6: 'fail to reject' does not mean 'accept'. p = 0.62 means the data are consistent with μ = $50,000, but also with many other values; the test may lack power.

exam.concept: Hypothesis test examples: GDP growth (Section 4.5, Key Concept 4.7)
exam.stem: The chapter tests H₀: μ = 2.0 for U.S. real GDP per capita growth, using 241 quarterly observations of annual growth (1960 to early 2020). The mean is 1.99%, t = −0.07, and p = 0.95. Which statements are justified? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The test establishes that average growth over the period was exactly 2.0% per year.
options.feedback: Revisit what a test can establish when it does not reject (Key Concept 4.6).

options.text: The test gives no evidence that average growth differed from 2.0% per year.
options.feedback: Correct: p = 0.95 gives no evidence against 2.0%.

options.text: Because 1.99% is below 2.0%, growth fell significantly short of the benchmark.
options.feedback: Revisit how the test judges a gap relative to its standard error (Section 4.4).

options.text: The average growth rate differs from 2.0% by about 0.07 percentage points.
options.feedback: Revisit what the t-statistic measures (Section 4.4).

options.text: Neighboring quarters' growth rates are strongly correlated, a feature the simple t-test ignores.
options.feedback: Correct: the chapter flags this time-series issue.

exam.explanation: Key Concepts 4.6 and 4.7: p = 0.95 means the data give no evidence against 2.0% growth, not that growth was exactly 2.0%. The gap itself is about 0.01 percentage points (t = −0.07 measures it in standard errors). The observations are quarterly and overlapping, so they are strongly autocorrelated, which the simple t-test ignores (Chapter 17).

exam.stem: For the women, the two-sided test of H₀: μ = $40,000 gives p = 0.4703, and the sample mean ($41,413) is above $40,000. What is the p-value of the upper-tailed test of H₀: μ ≤ $40,000 against Hₐ: μ > $40,000?

options.feedback: Revisit how many tails a one-sided p-value counts (Section 4.6).
Revisit which tail probability the upper-tailed p-value uses (Section 4.6).
Correct. With the sample mean on the Hₐ side, the one-sided p-value is half the two-sided one.
Revisit how the one-sided p-value relates to the two-sided one (Key Concept 4.8).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 4.8: p = Pr[T ≥ 0.72] = 0.2351, exactly half of 0.4703. It is still above 0.05, so H₀ is not rejected.

exam.stem: For the women, an analyst tests H₀: μ ≤ $40,000 against Hₐ: μ > $40,000 at α = 0.05 instead of the two-sided test of μ = $40,000. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Its critical value is 1.654 rather than ±1.974.
options.feedback: Correct: with 170 degrees of freedom, the 5% upper-tail cutoff is 1.654.

options.text: It effectively doubles the significance level to α = 0.10.
options.feedback: Revisit how a one-sided test uses α (Section 4.6).

options.text: It answers a directional question: whether mean earnings exceed $40,000.
options.feedback: Correct: the claim μ > $40,000 is the alternative hypothesis.

options.text: It may be chosen after the data show that the sample mean lies above $40,000.
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's warning about when the one-sided versus two-sided choice must be made (Section 4.6).

options.text: It uses the same t-statistic as the two-sided test.
options.feedback: Correct: t = (x̄ − 40,000)/se is unchanged; only the rejection region and p-value differ.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 4.8: a one-sided test uses the same t-statistic but puts all of α in one tail, so its critical value is smaller (1.654 versus ±1.974 here). The choice must be made before seeing the data.

exam.stem: An upper-tailed test of H₀: μ ≤ $40,000 against Hₐ: μ > $40,000 can also reject H₀ when the sample mean falls far below $40,000.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit where the rejection region of an upper-tailed test lies (Section 4.6).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. The rejection region lies only in the upper tail, so a sample mean far below $40,000 never rejects; one-sided tests cannot detect effects in the opposite direction.

exam.explanation: Section 4.4: one-sided tests have more power in the specified direction but cannot detect effects in the opposite direction. An upper-tailed test rejects only for large positive t.

exam.stem: In the chapter's poll, 480 of 921 voters intend to vote Democrat, so p̂ = 0.521. What is the standard error of p̂?

options.text: About 0.0165
About 0.500
options.feedback: Revisit the standard-error formula for a proportion in Section 4.7.

options.text: About 0.0003
options.feedback: Revisit the standard-error formula for a proportion in Section 4.7.

options.text: About 0.0005
options.feedback: Revisit the standard-error formula for a proportion in Section 4.7.

exam.explanation: Section 4.7: se(p̂) = √[p̂(1 − p̂)/n] = √(0.521 × 0.479/921) ≈ 0.0165, so the 95% margin of error is about 1.96 × 0.0165 ≈ 3.2 percentage points.

exam.stem: For the same poll (p̂ = 0.521, n = 921), the two-sided test of H₀: p = 0.50 gives a p-value of 0.20. What is the appropriate conclusion at α = 0.05?

options.text: The Democrat is ahead in the population, because 52.1% is above 50%.
options.feedback: Revisit how a test judges a sample gap against sampling variability (Section 4.7).

options.text: Reject H₀, because the sample proportion of 0.521 is above 0.50.
options.feedback: Revisit the decision rule based on the p-value (Section 4.4).

options.text: The race is exactly tied, because the test does not reject H₀.
options.feedback: Revisit what a non-rejection can establish (Key Concept 4.6).

options.text: Do not reject H₀: 52.1% of 921 voters is weak evidence against 50%.
options.feedback: Correct. p = 0.20 > 0.05, so a 50–50 split remains plausible.

exam.explanation: Section 4.7: p = 0.20 > 0.05, so H₀: p = 0.50 is not rejected; the 95% interval [48.9%, 55.3%] includes 50%. With the same 52% share but 2,500 voters, the gap would become significant.

exam.stem: In the poll, each voter is coded 1 for Democrat and 0 otherwise, so p̂ = 0.521 is the sample median of these 0/1 values.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit which summary of 0/1 data gives the fraction of 1s (Key Concept 4.9).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. p̂ is the sample mean of the 0/1 values; with more 1s than 0s, their median would be 1.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 4.9: a sample proportion is the sample mean of binary data, which is why the inference tools for means carry over to proportions.
